newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mbeki says whites stalling change in S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: Mbeki says whites stalling change in S.Africa.

text.p: Deputy President Thabo Mbeki said on Tuesday that South Africa's transition from apartheid was close to stalling and blamed whites for resisting change.

Mbeki, heir apparent to President Nelson Mandela and already in charge of the daily running of government, told parliament there was a growing tendency among whites to blame blacks for the failures of the first democratic government.
In one of his most critical speeches since the first all-race elections in April 1994, Mbeki said denying the damage of apartheid would not eliminate the need for change.
"Running like a structural fault through (post-apartheid South Africa) and weaving it together into a frightening bundle of imbalance and inequality, is the question of race and colour," Mbeki said.
"We are not far from the day when the diplomatic language will slip and the point will be made openly that 'the Bantus (blacks) are not yet ready to govern'."
Political analysts have interpreted Mbeki's recent speeches as the first signs of a resurgent Africanist tendency in the ruling African National Congress (ANC).

Party sources have confirmed that Africanists, who insist on the primacy of black Africans, complained at a special meeting recently that whites, ethnic Indians and mixed-race coloureds were too prominent in the party.
Mbeki said corruption caused by three centuries of white domination was to blame for social inequalities, apparently escalating crime, corruption and a lack of social values.
Whites hostile to change preferred to blame affirmative action, which was designed to accelerate equality by advancing blacks.
"Among many of us the mistaken assumption is made that the transition to a stable democracy has been completed," he said.

"This is a society which continues to be characterised by deep fissures which separate the black people from the white, the hungry from the prosperous, the urban from the rural, the male from the female, the disabled from the rest."

Mbeki accused whites of a "carefully calibrated amnesia about what our society has inherited from the past" and said South Africa could not build a sound moral foundation while whites continued to insist that apartheid was harmless.
Those who suggested that corruption was endemic to African governance and only as old as democracy in South Africa did nothing to help repair apartheid's damage, he said.

He also attacked what he identified as growing white hostility to Archbishop Desmond Tutu's statutory Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which is empowered to pardon offenders who freely confess to human rights offences under apartheid.

"The hatreds and animosities of the past will not go away unless the truth is told about what happened... We are diminished by the acts which occurred and not by their recounting to the commission and the nation.
"The recognition of the guilt is a necessary part of the commitment to the future not to repeat the past," he said.
